title: The reality of war: The Charge of the Light Brigade, Bayonet Charge, Remains and Kamikaze
specPoints: Paper 2 Section B: Power and Conflict: The Charge of the Light Brigade, Bayonet Charge, Remains, Kamikaze
AO2: voice, rhythm and structure; AO3: war and its aftermath

tips.title: Two charges, two aftermaths
tips.body: The Charge and Bayonet Charge for the moment of battle; Remains and Kamikaze for what follows it.

tips.title: Voice decides distance
tips.body: Third-person praise in Tennyson; close to one mind in Hughes; first person in Remains; a daughter's retelling in Kamikaze.

tips.title: Endings to quote
tips.body: Honour the Light Brigade; his bloody life in my bloody hands; which had been the better way to die.

tips.title: Offer readings
tips.body: The Charge can be read as celebration and quiet criticism; Bayonet Charge as patriotism exposed; say which lines allow it.

why.matters: These four poems cover the widest range of attitudes to war in the cluster: a laureate honouring obedience, a modern poet stripping away ideals, and two poems about what survivors carry. June 2024 asked about the ways people are affected by conflict, and these are the poems that answer it most directly. Comparing their voices, from praise at a distance to guilt in the first person, is the clearest route to the top level.

examples.title: Remembrance and questions
examples.body: Every November the dead of wars are honoured, and every generation also asks whether they were well led. The Charge of the Light Brigade does both at once, and the argument about what it means is still going on.

examples.title: The war that comes home
examples.body: Soldiers returning from recent wars have spoken of memories that return uninvited. Remains was written from such accounts, and its present tense is the sound of a memory that is not over.

steps.title: The Charge of the Light Brigade: glory and a blunder
steps.body:
Alfred, Lord Tennyson, the Poet Laureate, wrote the poem in 1854, weeks after the Battle of Balaclava in the Crimean War, when a misunderstood order sent about six hundred British cavalry charging into Russian guns. Newspaper reports of the charge spoke of a blunder.

> Half a league, half a league,\
>  Half a league onward,\
> All in the valley of Death\
>  Rode the six hundred.\
> "Forward, the Light Brigade!\
> "Charge for the guns!" he said:\
> Into the valley of Death\
>  Rode the six hundred.
>
> "Forward, the Light Brigade!"\
> Was there a man dismay'd?\
> Not tho' the soldier knew\
>  Some one had blunder'd:\
> Their's not to make reply,\
> Their's not to reason why,\
> Their's but to do and die,\
> Into the valley of Death\
>  Rode the six hundred.
>
> Cannon to right of them,\
> Cannon to left of them,\
> Cannon in front of them\
>  Volley'd and thunder'd;\
> Storm'd at with shot and shell,\
> Boldly they rode and well,\
> Into the jaws of Death,\
> Into the mouth of Hell\
>  Rode the six hundred.
>
> Flash'd all their sabres bare,\
> Flash'd as they turn'd in air,\
> Sabring the gunners there,\
> Charging an army, while\
>  All the world wonder'd:\
> Plunged in the battery-smoke\
> Right thro' the line they broke;\
> Cossack and Russian\
> Reel'd from the sabre-stroke\
>  Shatter'd and sunder'd.\
> Then they rode back, but not\
>  Not the six hundred.
>
> Cannon to right of them,\
> Cannon to left of them,\
> Cannon behind them\
>  Volley'd and thunder'd;\
> Storm'd at with shot and shell,\
> While horse and hero fell,\
> They that had fought so well\
> Came thro' the jaws of Death\
> Back from the mouth of Hell,\
> All that was left of them,\
>  Left of six hundred.
>
> When can their glory fade?\
> O the wild charge they made!\
>  All the world wonder'd.\
> Honour the charge they made!\
> Honour the Light Brigade,\
>  Noble six hundred!

**Rhythm.** “Half a league, half a league”: a stressed syllable and two unstressed, over and over, like hoofbeats. The poem gallops.

**Duty.** “Some one had blunder'd”, and yet “Their's not to reason why, Their's but to do and die”. The soldiers' obedience is the poem's praise, and its question.

**Repetition.** “Cannon to right of them, Cannon to left of them”: the guns surround them. “Into the jaws of Death, Into the mouth of Hell”.

**The ending.** “Then they rode back, but not Not the six hundred”, and then the command to the reader: “Honour the Light Brigade”, “Noble six hundred!”

steps.title: Bayonet Charge: one soldier, no glory
steps.body:
Ted Hughes published *Bayonet Charge* in 1957. It follows one soldier in a charge, apparently in the First World War; Hughes's father had fought in that war. The poem is in copyright, so it is quoted in short phrases.

**It starts in the middle.** “Suddenly he awoke and was running”: no scene is set, and the reader is thrown into the charge with him, in “raw-seamed hot khaki”.

**The body.** “Bullets smacking the belly out of the air”; “He lugged a rifle numb as a smashed arm”. The language is physical and violent.

**The ideals drop away.** “King, honour, human dignity, etcetera” “dropped like luxuries”: patriotic words become useless things to shed in a crisis.

**The hare.** “a yellow hare that rolled like a flame” in a “threshing circle”: nature, too, is caught and suffering.

**Terror.** He runs on with “his terror's touchy dynamite”.

Smacking the belly out of the air

steps.title: Remains: the soldier who cannot forget
steps.body:
Simon Armitage wrote *Remains* for *The Not Dead* (2008), a project giving voice to soldiers who had served in recent wars; it draws on a soldier's account of service in Iraq. It is in copyright, so it is quoted in short phrases.

**A casual voice.** “On another occasion”: the poem begins as if telling an anecdote. Three soldiers fire on a looter leaving a bank, “probably armed, possibly not”: “all three of us open fire”. The shared blame is in “myself and somebody else and somebody else”.

**The body.** He sees the man “sort of inside out”; someone “tosses his guts back into his body”. The slang is shockingly offhand.

**The turn.** “End of story, except not really”. The poem moves into the present tense: “he's here in my head when I close my eyes”; the memory is “dug in behind enemy lines”.

**The ending.** “his bloody life in my bloody hands”: the guilt is his own.

steps.title: Kamikaze: a pilot who turned back
steps.body:
Beatrice Garland's *Kamikaze* was published in 2013 and was printed in full on the June 2024 paper. Kamikaze pilots in the Second World War were Japanese airmen sent to crash their planes into enemy ships, a death presented as an honour. The poem is in copyright, so it is quoted in short phrases here.

**The departure.** “Her father embarked at sunrise”, a samurai sword, a shaven head “full of powerful incantations”, and “enough fuel for a one-way journey into history”.

**What he saw.** Looking down, fishing boats “strung out like bunting”; shoals of fish; memories of his father's boat and of a tuna, “the dark prince, muscular, dangerous”. The sea, life and home call him back. He turns round.

**The cost.** His wife never spoke to him again; neighbours treated him as if he no longer existed; then the children “we too learned to be silent”, and he was “no longer the father we loved”.

**The ending.** She says he must have wondered “which had been the better way to die”.

**Voice.** Told in the third person by a daughter to her own children, and shifting into her own voice, *my mother*, for the family's silence.

check.prompt: Why does the family's silence matter in Kamikaze?
check.solution: He turned back towards life, and his family and neighbours acted as if he no longer existed. His daughter's last line asks which had been the better way to die: in the plane, or in the silence.

steps.body: Two charges: one of six hundred, one of a single man.

visuals.problem: Compare how poets present the experience of a charge.

steps.text: Idea: Tennyson celebrates the courage of a group obeying a blunder; Hughes strips courage away and shows one terrified body.
Voice: Tennyson's third-person narrator praises from outside, “Rode the six hundred”, “Noble six hundred!”
steps.note: The soldiers are a heroic number, seen from a distance.

steps.text: Hughes stays close to one man: “Suddenly he awoke and was running”.
Ideals: Tennyson's soldiers keep them, “Their's not to reason why, Their's but to do and die”; Hughes's man drops them, “King, honour, human dignity, etcetera” “dropped like luxuries”.
Rhythm: a galloping dactyl in Tennyson, “Half a league, half a league”; broken, run-on lines in Hughes.
Judgement: Tennyson wrote for a nation reading about its soldiers; Hughes, a century later, asks what the charge felt like inside, and the answer is terror.

steps.title: The aftermath: Remains and Kamikaze
steps.body:
Two poems about what happens after the fighting, which the June 2024 question asked about.

**Remains:** the soldier survives and is haunted, in his own voice, in the present tense: “he's here in my head when I close my eyes”.

**Kamikaze:** the pilot survives and is shut out, seen through his daughter: “we too learned to be silent”.

**Guilt and shame.** Armitage's soldier carries guilt for a killing he did; Garland's pilot carries shame for a death he refused. One is haunted by what he did, the other judged for what he would not do.

**Endings.** Both end on death that goes on: blood on the hands, and the question of which death was better.

steps.title: Plan: Kamikaze and The Charge of the Light Brigade
steps.body:
Try: *Compare how poets present ideas about duty in 'Kamikaze' and 'The Charge of the Light Brigade'.*

1. The idea: duty demands death in both; Tennyson honours those who obey, Garland shows the cost of one who did not.
2. Voice: a praising narrator; a daughter's retelling.
3. Imagery: the valley of Death; the sea, the fish, the dark prince.
4. Endings: honour the six hundred; which had been the better way to die.
5. Context: Victorian Britain and the Crimea; Japan in 1944 and 1945.

Then write the paragraph on endings.

steps.title: Context and interpretation
steps.body:
**Tennyson, 1854.** As Poet Laureate he wrote for the nation. The poem honours the men, and “Some one had blunder'd” admits that the order was wrong; readers still argue whether it is a celebration, an elegy or a quiet criticism.

**Hughes, 1957.** Writing after two world wars, and with a father who had fought in the first, Hughes shows war from inside the body.

**Armitage, 2008.** Written from soldiers' own accounts of recent wars, at a time when the mental cost of service, post-traumatic stress, was more widely recognised.

**Garland, 2013.** A British poet imagining a Japanese story: duty, honour and a family's shame, told with sympathy.

Offer interpretations as readings: *it can be read as*, *many readers*, *the poem allows*.

steps.title: The reality of war in one page
steps.body:
Four poems about what war does: in the charge, and after.

- **The Charge of the Light Brigade (Tennyson, 1854):** galloping rhythm; a blunder; do and die; honour the six hundred.
- **Bayonet Charge (Hughes, 1957):** suddenly he awoke; the body; ideals dropped like luxuries; the yellow hare.
- **Remains (Armitage, 2008):** a casual anecdote; three open fire; end of story, except not really; blood on his hands.
- **Kamikaze (Garland, 2013):** a one-way journey; the sea and memory; the turn home; silence; which death was better.
- **Pairs:** the two charges; the two aftermaths; Kamikaze with The Charge on duty.

questions.prompt: Compare how poets present the ways people are affected by conflict in 'Kamikaze' and in 'Remains'. Write the opening idea and one integrated paragraph on endings.
questions.solution: Both poems show a man who survives conflict and is not freed by surviving: Armitage's soldier is haunted by what he did, Garland's pilot is judged for what he would not do. The endings make the difference sharp. Remains closes in the soldier's own voice: “his bloody life in my bloody hands”. The repeated *bloody* is both slang and literal, so the casual voice that began “On another occasion” cannot keep the horror at a distance any longer, and the guilt is his alone, in the present. Kamikaze closes in reported speech: she said he must have wondered “which had been the better way to die”. The daughter who “we too learned to be silent” gives her father the last thought, but only at a remove, as a question. Armitage, writing from soldiers' own accounts of recent wars, makes the reader live inside the memory; Garland, imagining a Japanese family for whom a returning kamikaze pilot was a disgrace, makes the reader watch a man become a ghost in his own home. Remains ends on certainty of guilt; Kamikaze ends on an uncertainty that is worse, because the choice he made for life cost him the life he chose.

questions.prompt: Write one analytical paragraph on how Tennyson presents the soldiers in 'The Charge of the Light Brigade'.
questions.skill: The Charge of the Light Brigade
questions.solution: Tennyson presents the soldiers as a single heroic body, obedient to the end. The rhythm of “Half a league, half a league” gallops, carrying the reader into the charge with them, and the refrain “Rode the six hundred” turns them into a number the poem honours. The poem admits the mistake, “Some one had blunder'd”, and at once sets their obedience above it: “Their's not to reason why, Their's but to do and die”. Repetition surrounds them with danger, “Cannon to right of them, Cannon to left of them”, and the paired images “Into the jaws of Death, Into the mouth of Hell” make the valley a mouth that swallows them. The ending counts the cost, “Then they rode back, but not Not the six hundred”, and then turns to the reader with an imperative, “Honour the Light Brigade”. Written by the Poet Laureate for a nation reading newspaper reports of the blunder, the poem can be read as a celebration that also lets criticism in: the men are noble, and someone sent them to die.

examTechnique.body:
**Know the attitude of each.** Honour, disillusion, guilt, shame.

**Compare voice.** It decides how close the reader stands.

**Short, exact lines for the copyrighted poems.** Only the named poem is printed.

**Context in a sentence each.** 1854 and a laureate; a father in the First World War; recent wars and soldiers' accounts; Japan in the Second World War.
examinerErrors: Saying all war poems are simply anti-war.
Missing the blunder in The Charge.
Retelling Kamikaze without the voice or the ending.
Treating Remains' slang as careless rather than chosen.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer on the war poems distinguishes attitudes, compares voice and ending, reads rhythm and slang as choices, offers interpretations grounded in lines, and ties each poem's context to a quotation.
